The primary weakness of the instruction lies in the overwhelmingly monotonous and one-directional teaching style. Classes are conducted almost entirely as uninterrupted monologues, with little variation in tone, pace, or method, which significantly reduces attention and engagement. Even subjects that are historically dynamic and intellectually stimulating are presented in a way that feels flat and distant, draining them of their analytical and narrative richness. Student participation is largely absent; questions are rarely encouraged, and when they occur, they are not developed into meaningful or thought-provoking discussions. The instructional approach relies heavily on reading from slides or directing students to external documentaries, which replaces rather than complements active teaching. This limits the development of critical, analytical, and independent thinking skills and positions students as passive recipients rather than active participants in the learning process.

Prof Aida is exceptional in explaining complex political science concepts in an accessible manner in the course. Besides valuing critical thinking in formulating opinions, she makes students practise precision when raising arguments in terms of formulating a viable alternative hypothesis as a critique of the arguments in the various papers discussed, specifying specific dependent and independent variables and causal mechanisms etc. As a political science undergraduate interested in comparative politics, this course has a been an excellent opportunity for me to practise technical skills I was taught in political science research in almost every lesson. In this way, this course has been a crucial stepping stone for me to pursue other comparative politics modules in my home university. Besides technical skills, Prof also makes it a point to draw connections (and encourage students to do the same) between themes and arguments discussed in the course. She shows students how to thinking about and critique arguments and in turn, students go through an iterative process by applying these new ways of thinking/critiquing across articles that discuss other concepts and themes. Prof Aida is also very knowledgeable in the field is able to provide many insights based on her vast experience in political research. Overall, this course is solid in terms of sharpening important skills for senior political science students while discussing important contemporary issues in comparative politics. Prof Aida also makes it a point to make the course comprehensive by exposing students to wide range of classic and recent cutting edge research therefore allowing students to track evolutions/developments and draw comparisons in ways researchers think about certain political science concepts. Finally, Prof Aida is also very kind and approachable with students: she goes above and beyond to check in on international students and how they are doing as well as find their way around the university :)
